title: Are forty and two hundred and thirty one co-prime?
description: The primes of forty are listed, then the primes of two hundred and thirty one, and the two lists are compared. Keeko doubts this and says they are not co-prime because neither number is prime.
teaching_notes: One idea: two numbers are co-prime when their lists of primes share nothing. Watch for students who think co-prime numbers must themselves be prime.

source: Consider 40 and 231. Their prime factorisations are 40 = 2 ×
video_script.why: The child sees that two numbers are co-prime when no prime is common to their prime factorisations.
video_script.substitution: the book's own numbers, forty and two hundred and thirty one
video_script.anchor: the rows of primes of forty and of two hundred and thirty one, with their lists of different primes beside them
video_script.wrong_answer: they are not co-prime because neither number is prime
video_script.wrong_move: Keeko thinks co-prime numbers must themselves be prime.
video_script.payoff_line: Forty and two hundred and thirty one are co-prime

final_answer.spoken: forty and two hundred and thirty one are co-prime

maths_rules: no prime is in both lists, so 40 and 231 are co-prime
8 = 2 × 2 × 2 and 9 = 3 × 3 are not prime but share no prime, so they are co-prime

narration: <bookmark mark='ans'/>Forty and two hundred and thirty one are co-prime. They have no common prime factor, so the only common factor is one.

narration: <bookmark mark='doubt'/>Keeko thinks they are not co-prime because neither number is prime.
<bookmark mark='eight'/>Look at eight and nine. Neither is prime, but they have no prime in common.
<bookmark mark='strike'/>Co-prime asks whether a prime is shared, never whether the numbers are prime.
